cards: Edward S. Morse finds cord-marked sherds and gives the culture its name
Johan Gunnar Andersson discovers the Yangshao site in western Henan, which gives the culture its name
The Yangshao culture is estimated to be more than 1,000 years older than the Anau culture, weakening Andersson’s theory of a western origin
The Japanese archaeologist Torii Ryūzō discovers the Hongshanhou site at Chifeng
Kōsaku Hamada and Mizuno Seiichi excavate Hongshanhou extensively
Shi Xingeng first excavates the type site at Liangzhu in Yuhang County, Zhejiang
The Zhejiang provincial government announces the discovery of the base of the ancient city walls, the centre of the culture
The new Liangzhu Culture Museum is completed and opens
The archaeological ruins of Liangzhu City are inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site
The Chengziya site near Longshan in Shandong is found, and excavated in 1930 and 1931
Kwang-chih Chang describes a uniform “Longshanoid horizon”, which he replaces in 1986 with a “Chinese interaction sphere” of regional cultures
Viktor Sarianidi names the complex the Bactria–Margiana Archaeological Complex
Xu Xusheng discovers the Erlitou site and suggests it was Bo, the first capital of the Shang
Radiocarbon studies narrow the culture’s dates to 1750–1500 BCE
The Erlitou Site Museum of the Xia Capital, with more than 2,000 objects from the site, opens in Luoyang
The state of Qin conquers the region of the kingdom of Shu
A farmer dredging an irrigation ditch unearths a large cache of jade objects
David Crockett Graham of West China Union University organises the first archaeological excavation
Local workers find two sacrificial pits filled with broken and burned gold, bronze, jade and pottery objects
The Sanxingdui Museum opens near the site
King Wu of Zhou defeats Di Xin at the Battle of Muye
The Late Mumun begins, with fewer, larger settlements, fortified hilltops such as Namsan and signs of conflict
Songguk-ri Culture pit-houses are found deep in the interior of Gangwon Province
A cult of Ganesha, the Elephant-Head God, is attested, as influences from the Indian subcontinent arrive with the spread of Buddhism
Kang Youwei persuades the emperor to order temples that perform no state sacrifices turned into schools; the confiscations are soon reversed
The Nationalist government’s “Standards for retaining or abolishing gods and shrines” try to abolish the cults of all gods but great heroes and sages
After the adoption of the new constitution the religion revives rapidly, with millions of temples rebuilt or built from scratch
The First Emperor of Qin standardises the Chinese script across his empire
Xu Shen completes the Shuowen Jiezi, the first dictionary to analyse the structure of characters
The Diamond Sutra in Chinese, the earliest dated printed book, is made in China
King Sejong of Korea promulgates the Hangul alphabet as an alternative to Chinese characters
The Kangxi Dictionary is completed, listing more than 47,000 characters
China’s Ministry of Education orders primary schools to teach the vernacular instead of Classical Chinese
Duke Huan takes the throne and appoints Guan Zhong as minister
Duke Huan presides over the covenant of Kuiqiu as hegemon
The Zhou king recognises Tian He as ruler of Qi
Sun Bin's strategy defeats Wei at the Battle of Maling
Yue Yi's coalition army sacks Linzi
Tian Dan breaks the siege of Jimo and restores Qi
King Jian surrenders to Qin, completing the Qin unification
King Wu defeats the Shang at the Battle of Muye
King Li is driven out and the Gonghe regency begins
King Xuan begins a revival against the Xianyun and the Huaiyi
The Quanrong and the Marquis of Shen sack Haojing and kill King You
Xiong Tong proclaims himself king as King Wu of Chu
King Zhuang defeats Jin at the Battle of Bi
The State of Wu defeats Chu at Boju and occupies Ying
Nobles kill the reformer Wu Qi after the death of King Dao
Bai Qi of Qin captures Ying; the capital moves to Chen
Chu moves its capital to Shouchun
The Qin general Wang Jian captures King Fuchu and annexes Chu
Duke Xiang escorts King Ping of Zhou east and is raised to full ducal rank
Duke Mu defeats Jin at Han and captures Duke Hui of Jin
Shang Yang begins his reforms under Duke Xiao
Qin conquers Ba and Shu in the Sichuan basin
Bai Qi destroys the army of Zhao at Changping
Zheng takes the title of First Emperor
King Ateas, who had extended his rule to the Danube, is killed fighting Philip II of Macedon
Qin unifies China, and the First Emperor orders new walls to join the fortifications of the northern frontier against the Xiongnu
The Portuguese Jesuit brother Bento de Góis reaches Jiayu Pass from India, perhaps the first recorded European entry into China through the wall
The Ming general Wu Sangui opens the gates of Shanhai Pass to the Manchus, who go on to consolidate Qing rule over China proper
The Great Wall is voted one of the New 7 Wonders of the World
A survey by the National Cultural Heritage Administration puts the walls and trenches at 21,196.18 km and the Ming wall at 8,850 km
Cyrus the Great dies fighting the Massagetae, according to Herodotus
Saka troops fight in the Persian centre at the Battle of Marathon
Alexander the Great defeats a Saka force at the Jaxartes
Yang Hu, a retainer of the Ji family, rebels and seizes power in Lu
After Yang Hu is expelled, Confucius is appointed governor of a town, later rising to Minister of Crime
Hou Fan's revolt at Hou opens the way for Confucius to press the three families to dismantle their strongholds
The walls of Hou and Bi are razed, but Duke Ding's siege of Cheng fails
Confucius leaves Lu and begins years of travel among the states of north-east and central China
The Sogdian Maniakh leads a Turkic embassy to the emperor Justin II in Constantinople
The Arabs under Qutayba ibn Muslim take Samarkand
Confucius is born in the state of Lu, by the traditional date
Confucius dies; his disciples gather his sayings, later compiled as the Analects
The Qin dynasty orders the burning of books, the Confucian classics among them, by the traditional account
Emperor Wu of Han establishes official chairs for the Five Classics
The Sui dynasty founds the imperial examinations, later based on the Confucian classics
Zhu Xi publishes the Four Books with his commentaries, the core of Neo-Confucianism
The Qing government abolishes the imperial examinations
Confucius dies; by tradition his disciples then collect and jointly edit their records of his conversations
He Yan's Collected Explanations of the Analects is written, for nearly 1,000 years the standard guide to the text
The Qi version, lost for about 1,800 years, is found in the tomb of the Marquis of Haihun
Zhang Daoling receives a revelation from the deified Laozi and founds the Way of the Celestial Masters
The Yellow Turban rebellion of the Way of Great Peace shakes the Han dynasty
The Northern Wei emperor Taiwu receives Daoist registers, making Daoism the religion of his state
The Tang emperor Gaozong honours Laozi, the dynasty’s claimed ancestor, as an emperor
Wang Chongyang founds the monastic school of Complete Perfection (Quanzhen)
The Quanzhen master Qiu Chuji meets Genghis Khan in the Hindu Kush
The Ming court completes the printing of the Daoist Canon
The Eastern Zhou dynasty is established, beginning the decline of Zhou authority that led to the Warring States period
The Han dynasty abolishes mutilating punishments, in continuity with Qin practice
The Book of Han lists the fa school among the categories of its catalogue
Herrlee G. Creel’s Legalists or Administrators? leads many scholars to avoid the term Legalism
The Xiongnu empire is founded, the first of a succession of steppe khanates and empires that practised Tengrism
The Secret History of the Mongols is written, tracing Genghis Khan’s line to Borte Chino, born with “destiny from Tengri”
Hulegu Khan writes from Maragheh to Louis IX of France, in a letter that treats Nestorian Christianity as part of the khans’ Tengrism
Dastan Sarygulov founds Tengir Ordo in Kyrgyzstan to promote the values and traditions of Tengrism
Modu seizes power from his father Touman and unites the Xiongnu
Modu surrounds Han Emperor Gaozu for seven days at the Battle of Baideng
The Han accept the heqin treaty of gifts and royal brides in exchange for peace
A failed Han ambush at Mayi ends the policy of appeasement
Wei Qing and Huo Qubing defeat the Xiongnu at the Battle of Mobei
Chanyu Huhanye travels to Chang'an and acknowledges Han overlordship
The confederation splits into Southern and Northern Xiongnu
The Northern Xiongnu suffer a crushing defeat by Han forces and their allies
The first ritual rebuilding of the Grand Shrine of Ise
The Kojiki records the myths of the kami and the descent of the emperors from the sun goddess
The Engishiki lists 2,861 shrines and the court’s rituals and prayers
The Meiji government orders the separation of kami and buddhas
The shrine later named Yasukuni is founded in Tokyo for those who died fighting for the emperor
The Allied occupation’s Shinto Directive ends State Shinto
The Na state of Wo receives a golden seal from Emperor Guangwu of the Later Han dynasty
Modu, once a hostage of the Yuezhi, seizes power among the Xiongnu
Work begins on the mausoleum of the future first emperor, then aged 13 and newly King of Qin
Farmers digging a well near Mount Li find the first figures, prompting archaeologists to investigate
The first exhibition of the figures outside China opens at the National Gallery of Victoria in Melbourne
Excavation of Pit K9901 uncovers the figures dubbed the Acrobats
A grave pit holding 121 skeletons attributed to the site’s workers is excavated
The British Museum opens “The First Emperor: China’s Terracotta Army”, which made 2008 its most successful year
Qin attacks the state of Han directly to its east and takes its capital city of Xinzheng, opening the wars of unification.
Qin conquers Qi, taking its capital at Linzi, and King Zheng declares himself Shi Huangdi, the First Emperor.
The general Meng Tian conquers the Ordos region from the Xiongnu and agriculture is established there.
Some 500,000 men are sent south against the Baiyue peoples; after heavy losses, Qin takes the coastal lands around Guangzhou and the provinces of Fuzhou and Guilin.
Qin Shi Huang dies on a journey to the eastern frontiers; Li Si and Zhao Gao hide his death, alter his will and place Huhai on the throne as Qin Er Shi.
Popular revolt breaks out as men across China attack officials, raise armies and declare themselves kings.
Ziying, a son of Fusu, surrenders to Liu Bang on his arrival at Xianyang and is soon executed by Xiang Yu.
Xianyang is destroyed, marking the end of the imperial Qin dynasty; the Chu–Han Contention follows.
Modu Chanyu takes power and unites the Xiongnu, founding the first great empire of the eastern steppe
After Emperor Gaozu’s defeat at Baideng, the Han buy peace with a princess and regular gifts of silk and grain
Amid a Xiongnu civil war, Huhanye pays homage in person at Chang’an and accepts Han overlordship
Bumin Qaghan overthrows the Rouran and founds the First Turkic Khaganate
A kurultai at the source of the Onon river proclaims Temüjin Genghis Khan of the Mongols
Rival kurultais elect Kublai Khan and Ariq Böke as Great Khan, and the Mongol Empire begins to break apart
Qing armies crush the last Dzungar resistance, ending the last great nomadic empire of the steppe
Liu Bang defeats Xiang Yu and proclaims himself emperor as Gaozu
Emperor Wu takes the throne, beginning the dynasty's most expansive reign
The Imperial Academy is founded to train officials in the Confucian classics
Wei Qing and Huo Qubing drive Xiongnu power beyond the Gobi Desert
The Han census records a population of nearly 60 million
The dynasty is restored as the Eastern Han after Wang Mang's usurpation
The Yellow Turban Rebellion erupts amid famine and peasant displacement
Cao Pi deposes Emperor Xian and declares the Wei dynasty, ending the Han
Xianbei warriors kill the Northern Xiongnu chanyu Youliu
Tanshihuai routs a three-pronged Han expedition into the steppe
Kebineng marches to Beidi in support of Zhuge Liang
Kebineng is assassinated on the orders of Wang Xiong of Cao Wei
The Xiongnu drive the Yuezhi from western Gansu and then overcome the Tarim statelets
After campaigns begun in 108 BCE, the Han dynasty establishes the Protectorate of the Western Regions under Zheng Ji
Kumārajīva of Kucha, captured in 384, is brought to Chang’an, where he heads a translation bureau until his death in 413
The monk Xuanzang visits Kucha and records about a hundred convents with more than five thousand monks
The Tang send an army under Ashina She’er, who takes Kucha and later has 11,000 of its people executed in reprisal for the killing of the protector-general
Menri monastery, the most important Bon monastery, is built in Tsang
Many Bonpos and Nyingmapas are executed during the Dzungar invasion of Tibet
China invades Tibet, where there are about 300 Bon monasteries; Bonpo scholars begin to reach Europe and North America
The Central Tibetan Administration in exile accepts Bon as a religious group with the same rights as the Buddhist schools
Traditional founding of Saro by Bak Hyeokgeose
King Beopheung recognises Buddhism after the martyrdom of Ichadon
King Jinheung seizes the Han River valley from Baekje
Silla conquers Daegaya, the last Gaya state
Silla and Tang destroy Baekje after the Battle of Hwangsanbeol
Silla and Tang take Pyongyang and destroy Goguryeo
Victory at Gibeolpo ends the Silla–Tang War
King Gyeongsun surrenders Silla to Goryeo
Traditional founding of Goguryeo by Jumong at Jolbon
Goguryeo captures the Lelang commandery, ending Chinese rule around Pyongyang
Buddhism is received and the Taehak academy founded under King Sosurim
King Jangsu erects the stele of Gwanggaeto the Great at Ji'an
The capital moves from Gungnae to Pyongyang
Jangsu takes the Baekje capital Hanseong
Eulji Mundeok routs a Sui army at the Salsu River
Tang and Silla forces take Pyongyang; the kingdom ends
Traditional founding of Baekje by Onjo at Wiryeseong
Geunchogo's army kills the Goguryeo king Gogugwon at Pyongyang
The monk Marananta brings Buddhism from the Eastern Jin
Goguryeo takes Hanseong; the court moves to Ungjin
King Seong moves the capital to Sabi
King Seong is killed fighting Silla at Gwansanseong
Silla and Tang take Sabi; King Uija surrenders
Tang and Silla defeat Baekje loyalists and a Yamato fleet at Baekgang
A Kushan army crossing the Pamirs is repulsed by the Han general Ban Chao
An embassy from the Kushan king, probably Vasudeva I, reaches the Wei court
Sima Rui takes the imperial title at Jiankang as Emperor Yuan
Huan Wen conquers the Cheng Han state in Sichuan
Wang Xizhi writes his preface at the Orchid Pavilion gathering
Jin forces defeat the Former Qin at the Battle of Fei River
Sun En's Daoist rebellion breaks out in the coastal south
Huan Xuan usurps the throne as emperor of Chu
Liu Yu's army conquers the Later Qin and takes Chang'an
Emperor Gong abdicates to Liu Yu, founder of the Liu Song
Shelun takes the title khagan after conquering the Gaoche
Rouran cavalry raid the Northern Wei centre of Shengle
Emperor Taiwu of Northern Wei routs the khagan Datan in Mongolia
The Rouran install Kan Bozhou as king of Gaochang
The Gaoche break away under Afuzhiluo
Anagui flees to the Northern Wei, which later restores him
Bumin's Turks defeat the Rouran; Anagui kills himself
The last Rouran refugees are killed at Chang'an
The Huns arrive on the Volga, setting the Goths and Alans moving westward.
The Huns make their first large-scale attack on the Eastern Roman Empire, overrunning Armenia and pillaging Cappadocia and Thrace, and invade the Sasanian Empire, where they are badly defeated.
The brothers Attila and Bleda force the Eastern Roman Empire to sign the Treaty of Margus, granting the Huns trade rights and an annual tribute.
Attila, sole ruler since Bleda's death in 445, invades the Balkans and Thrace; the war ends in 449 with a tribute of 2,100 pounds of gold a year.
Attila's forces enter Gaul, attack Metz and besiege Orléans; a combined Roman and Visigothic army fights them at the Battle of the Catalaunian Plains.
Attila dies of a haemorrhage on his wedding night, having sacked northern Italy the year before and met Pope Leo I near Mantua.
At the Battle of Nedao the Gepid king Ardaric leads a Germanic coalition against Attila's son Ellak; the Huns lose many of their Germanic vassals.
Dengizich is defeated and killed in Thrace; the Huns are absorbed by other peoples such as the Bulgars.
Tuoba Gui reasserts Tuoba independence as Prince of Dai and then Prince of Wei, as Former Qin breaks apart after the Battle of Fei River.
Tuoba Gui inflicts a heavy defeat on the Later Yan crown prince Murong Bao at the Battle of Canhe Slope; the Central Plains are overrun and Yan splits in two.
Emperor Taiwu conquers the Northern Liang in the Hexi Corridor, unifying northern China and ending the Sixteen Kingdoms period.
Emperor Wen of Liu Song's great invasion is lured across the Yellow River and destroyed; Wei armies devastate the provinces to the south until January 451.
Emperor Xiaowen moves the capital from Pingcheng to Luoyang and pursues systematic sinicisation; the Tuoba take the surname Yuan.
Empress Dowager Hu poisons the young Emperor Xiaoming; the warlord Erzhu Rong butchers some 2,000 courtiers in the Heyin massacre and throws her into the Yellow River.
The first Hephthalite embassy reaches the Chinese court of the Northern Wei; twenty-four embassies to China are recorded in all, the last in 558.
The Hephthalite king Akhshunwar helps Peroz I gain the Sasanian throne from his brother.
Peroz I begins three wars against his former allies; captured in the first two, he pays thirty mules loaded with silver drachms and leaves his son Kavad as a hostage.
At the Battle of Herat Peroz I is defeated and killed by the Hephthalite king Kun-khi; for two years the Hephthalites plunder and control the eastern Sasanian Empire.
A Hephthalite army defeats the Sasanian army of Balash and places Kavad I, who had lived four years among the Hephthalites, on the throne.
The Hephthalites capture Sughd, the capital of Sogdiana, and push north of Turfan to the Urumchi region in the Tarim Basin.
King Yilituo Yandai sends the first Hephthalite ambassador to the Southern Liang court, recorded in the Portraits of Periodical Offering of Liang.

The Turks of the First Turkic Khaganate and the Sasanians under Khosrow I defeat the Hephthalites after an eight-day battle near Qarshi, the Battle of Gol-Zarriun; the empire breaks into principalities.
Bumin destroys the Rouran and declares himself Qaghan of the Turks
The Gokturks send their first embassy to Constantinople, led by the Sogdian Maniakh
Gokturk forces reach the Crimea and besiege the Byzantine city of Bosporus
Tang China conquers the Eastern Khaganate and captures Illig Qaghan
Ilterish Qaghan founds the Second Khaganate through guerrilla warfare
Bilge Qaghan is poisoned by one of his own ministers
Uyghurs, Karluks and Basmyls seize Otuken and kill the last Gokturk qaghan
Yang Jian, regent for the child Emperor Jing of Northern Zhou, usurps the throne as Emperor Wen and names his dynasty Sui, after a bloody purge of 59 Zhou princes.
The Sui amass 518,000 troops along the northern bank of the Yangtze River, from Sichuan to the East China Sea, against the Chen dynasty.
Sui troops enter Jiankang and the last emperor of Chen surrenders; the city is razed and China proper is reunified.
Emperor Wen has relics of the Buddha distributed to temples throughout China, presenting himself as a Cakravartin king in imitation of Ashoka.
The Sui retake the Hanoi area from the Early Lý ruler Lý Phật Tử, opening the Linyi-Champa Campaign of 602–605.
Emperor Yang moves the capital to Luoyang, re-founded as a planned city, and enormously enlarges the Grand Canal works.
The last of four massive expeditions against Goguryeo ends in failure, leaving a deficit of money and men from which the Sui never recover.
Emperor Yang is assassinated by the minister Yuwen Huaji; in the north Li Yuan rises and takes the throne as Emperor Gaozu of Tang.
Li Yuan proclaims the Tang Dynasty after seizing Chang'an from the collapsing Sui
Li Shimin kills his brothers at the Xuanwu Gate and becomes Emperor Taizong
The Tang destroy the Eastern Turkic Khaganate; Taizong is hailed as Heavenly Khagan
Wu Zetian proclaims her own Zhou dynasty, interrupting Tang rule until 705
Abbasid forces defeat Gao Xianzhi's Tang army at the Battle of Talas
An Lushan rebels, capturing Luoyang and Chang'an and forcing Xuanzong to flee
Zhu Wen deposes the last Tang emperor and founds the Later Liang
Princess Wencheng of Tang China arrives as a bride for the Tibetan royal house
Tibet conquers the Tuyuhun around Lake Kokonor
Tibetans defeat a Tang army at the Dafei River and overrun the Tarim Basin
A Tibetan army occupies the Tang capital Chang'an for about two weeks
Emperor Udumtsen (Langdarma) is assassinated and the empire breaks apart
Wu is born to Wu Shiyue and Lady Yang, in the seventh year of the reign of Emperor Gaozu of Tang
Emperor Taizong dies and Wu, his childless concubine, is consigned to Ganye Temple as a Buddhist nun
Emperor Gaozong deposes Empress Wang and makes Wu empress
Gaozong falls ill and has Wu rule on the daily petitions of officials
Gaozong dies at Luoyang; Wu keeps real authority as empress dowager and regent
She changes the state's name to Zhou and takes the throne as emperor
She recalls her son Li Zhe from exile and makes him crown prince
A coup in February forces her to yield the throne and restores the Tang; she dies in December
The Khazars destroy an Arab army at Marj Ardabil
Marwan ibn Muhammad's great campaign forces a temporary Khazar submission
Dae Joyeong defeats a Tang army at Tianmenling and founds the state of Jin
Tang recognises Dae Joyeong as Commandery Prince of Bohai
The first Balhae embassy reaches Japan
A Balhae fleet raids Dengzhou in Shandong
King Seon begins a reign of northern expansion
King Dae Inseon surrenders to the Khitan; Balhae becomes the client state of Dongdan
Bumin founds the Turkic Khaganate, the first state to bear the name Türk
The memorial inscription of Kul Tigin is raised in the Orkhon valley
The fall of the Uyghur Khaganate drives the Uyghurs to the oases of Turfan and Gansu
Yusuf Khass Hajib completes the Kutadgu Bilig, the first great Islamic work in Turkic
Vilhelm Thomsen deciphers the Old Turkic runic script
The Basmyls capture Ötüken and kill Özmiş Khagan; a Uyghur–Karluk alliance then destroys the Basmyls, and Kutlug I Bilge Khagan builds his capital at Ordu-Baliq.
The Uyghurs kill Kulun Beg, the last khagan of the Göktürks, and send his head to the Tang.
About 4,000 Uyghur horsemen under Bayanchur Khan's eldest son help Tang armies retake Chang'an and Luoyang; the Uyghurs loot Luoyang for three days.
Bögü Qaghan helps defeat the rebels at Luoyang, sacks the city, and is converted by Manichaean priests; Manichaeism becomes the official religion.
Tun Baga Tarkhan kills his nephew Bögü Qaghan and nearly two thousand of his family, clique and Sogdians, takes the throne and suppresses Manichaeism.
Baoyi Qaghan defeats the Tibetans and Karluks and takes Gaochang; a Tibetan force besieging Yushu is destroyed.
Qutluq Bilge Qaghan dies and the Yaghlakar dynasty ends; the general Qutluq II declares himself qaghan, founding the Ädiz dynasty.
Invited by the minister Kulug Bagha, some 80,000 Yenisei Kyrgyz horsemen sack Ordu-Baliq, behead Qasar Qaghan and burn the empire's cities.
The Samanid amir Ismail ibn Ahmad captures Talas
Chroniclers record the conversion of 200,000 tents of Turks to Islam
Nasr ibn Ali takes Bukhara and ends the Samanid Empire
Mahmud of Ghazni defeats the Kara-Khanids near Balkh
Mahmud of Ghazni invades Ghor and captures its chief, Muhammad ibn Suri
Mu'izz al-Din takes Ghazni and makes it his base for campaigns in India
The Ghurids take Lahore, ending Ghaznavid rule
Mu'izz al-Din defeats Prithviraj Chauhan at the Second Battle of Tarain
The Khwarazmshah and the Qara Khitai defeat Mu'izz al-Din at Andkhud
Mu'izz al-Din is assassinated; Qutb al-Din Aybak takes power at Lahore
The Khwarazmian Empire takes Ghazni, ending Ghurid rule
Abaoji proclaims himself emperor of the Khitan
The Khitan destroy Balhae and set up the client kingdom of Dongdan
Later Jin hands over the Sixteen Prefectures around modern Beijing
Yelü Deguang takes Kaifeng and adopts the dynastic name Liao
The Treaty of Chanyuan brings annual Song payments of silver and silk
The wooden Sakyamuni Pagoda at Yingxian is completed
Wanyan Aguda proclaims the Jin dynasty and routs the Liao at Hubudagang
The Jin capture the last Liao emperor, Tianzuo
Wang Geon is raised to the throne and founds Goryeo
Taejo defeats Later Baekje, completing the reunification of the peninsula
Gang Gam-chan destroys a Khitan army at the Battle of Gwiju
Military officers seize power and depose King Uijong
The court withdraws to Ganghwa Island during the Mongol invasions
Carving of the Tripitaka Koreana woodblocks is completed
Yi Seong-gye deposes King Gongyang and founds Joseon
Zhao Kuangyin seizes power in the Chenqiao Mutiny and founds the Song Dynasty
The Chanyuan Treaty commits the Song to annual silk and silver payments to the Liao
Wang Anshi launches the New Policies to reform state finances
The Jurchen Jin capture Kaifeng and carry off emperors Huizong and Qinzong
Southern Song fleets defeat the Jin at Tangdao and Caishi
The Mongols begin the five-year siege of Xiangyang
Lin'an surrenders and the boy emperor Gong is taken north
The loyalist fleet is destroyed at Yamen, ending the Song Dynasty
Sabuktigin is chosen as leader of the Turkic garrison at Ghazni
Mahmud takes Khurasan and is recognised by the Abbasid caliph
Mahmud defeats the Hindu Shahi king Jayapala near Peshawar
Mahmud sacks the temple of Somnath
The Seljuks defeat Mas'ud I at the Battle of Dandanaqan
The Ghurids take Lahore, ending the dynasty
An entry in Murasaki's diary refers to the tale, the oldest dated reference to it
The author of the Sarashina Nikki records her joy at acquiring a complete copy of over 50 chapters
Suematsu Kenchō publishes the first, partial English translation, of seventeen chapters
Edward Seidensticker publishes the first complete English translation
An original copy of the fifth chapter, Wakamurasaki, in Fujiwara Teika's hand is found in Tokyo
Li Yuanhao declares himself emperor of the Great Xia at Xingqing, taking the Tangut clan name Weiming and creating a Chinese-style bureaucracy.
After victories at Sanchuan Pass and Haoshuichuan and the repulse of a Liao invasion of 100,000, Jingzong makes peace: the Song recognise him and pay 250,000 units of silk, silver and tea a year.
The Song launch a five-pronged invasion while the Liang clan imprisons Emperor Huizong; Lanzhou falls, but the Xia flood the Song camps by breaching the Yellow River dikes.
Empress Dowager Liang, who led armies in person, is poisoned by assassins from the Liao; the Song 'advance and fortify' campaign has built 40 forts across the Ordos.
Emperor Chongzong turns away the fugitive Liao emperor Tianzuo and declares himself a vassal of the Jurchen Jin.
Emperor Renzong institutes imperial examinations, after founding schools throughout the country and Confucian temples.
After the Mongol siege of Zhongxing, Emperor Xiangzong submits to Genghis Khan, giving him his daughter Chaka and a tribute of camels, falcons and textiles.
Emperor Mo surrenders after a six-month siege and is executed; the Mongols slaughter the capital's population and plunder the imperial tombs.
Wanyan Aguda proclaims the Great Jin
Jin capture the Liao emperor Tianzuo, ending the Liao state
Jin take Kaifeng and carry off two Song emperors
The Treaty of Shaoxing fixes the Song border on the Huai River
Prince Hailing moves the capital to Zhongdu (Beijing)
Genghis Khan invades and defeats the Jin at Yehuling
Caizhou falls and Emperor Aizong takes his own life
Yelü Dashi flees north-west to the garrison of Kedun on the Orkhon River, wins the allegiance of its 20,000 troops and proclaims himself gurkhan.
Dashi conquers the Karakhanid city of Balasaghun; the Kankalis, Karluks, Kyrgyz and the Kingdom of Qocho become vassals, while a Khitan attack on the Jin ends in disaster.
On 9 September the Khitans destroy Ahmad Sanjar's Seljuk army at the Battle of Qatwan north of Samarkand; Transoxiana is lost to the Seljuks and Khwarazm becomes a vassal.
Yelü Dashi dies; his wife Xiao Tabuyan rules as regent with the titles of empress Gantian, Gurkhan and Dashi.
The Qara Khitai cross the Amu Darya to defeat Khwarazm for unpaid tribute and install Tekish as Khwarazm Shah on 11 December.
A Qara Khitai army invading Ghurid lands near Kurzuban is routed in a night attack with 12,000 losses; Balkh passes to the Ghurids.
The Naiman refugee Kuchlug, married to Yelü Zhilugu's daughter, revolts and captures the gurkhan while he is hunting; Zhilugu remains nominal ruler until his death two years later.
Pursued by Genghis Khan's general Jebe, Kuchlug is captured and decapitated; the Mongols complete the conquest of the former Qara Khitai lands by 1220.
He joins a Jin campaign against the Tatars and helps Toghrul to regain the lordship of the Kereit
Attacked by Toghrul and defeated at Qalaqaljid Sands, he regroups at Baljuna and overpowers the Kereit
An assembly at the source of the Onon River sees him formally adopt the title Genghis Khan
The Jin capital Zhongdu surrenders after a four-year campaign and is sacked
He invades the Khwarazmian Empire after the killing of his envoy
He dies in August while subduing the Western Xia, whose capital falls the following month
Goryeo’s generals seize power in Korea and rule through their council while kings reign as figureheads
Soldiers expel England’s Rump Parliament; army officers draft a constitution making Oliver Cromwell Lord Protector
Spaniards form local and national juntas to resist Napoleon’s invasion, the councils from which the modern term derives
Colonels seize power in Greece and rule until their coup in Cyprus brings their fall in 1974
The commanders of Chile’s army, navy, air force and police seize power and rule as a junta until 1990
Ethiopia’s military council, the Derg, deposes Emperor Haile Selassie and rules until 1987
Argentina’s armed forces seize power; defeat in the Falklands War of 1982 forces them to hold elections in 1983
Myanmar’s armed forces seize power in a coup on 1 February, their third takeover since 1958
A Jesuit Latin manuscript first records the name, as Aino, and calls Hokkaido “Aino moxori”
The Meiji government sets up the Hokkaidō Development Commission to settle Hokkaido
The Hokkaido Former Aborigines Protection Act takes Ainu land and aims to erase Ainu culture and identity
The Sapporo District Court’s Nibutani Dam ruling recognises the Ainu as an Indigenous people, and the Ainu Culture Law replaces the 1899 act
The National Diet passes an act recognising the Ainu as an Indigenous people of Japan
Temüjin is proclaimed Genghis Khan at a kurultai on the Mongolian steppe
Subutai and Jebe defeat the Rus and Kipchaks at the Kalka River
Mongol armies defeat Polish and Hungarian forces at Legnica and Mohi
Hülegü sacks Baghdad, ending the Abbasid Caliphate
Kublai's death removes the last Great Khan widely recognised across the empire
The Ming drive the Yuan dynasty out of China
Genghis Khan adopts a script for the Mongolian language, adapted from the Uyghur alphabet
The Soyombo alphabet is created for Buddhist texts
Cyrillic is made mandatory in the Mongolian state, after a Latin alphabet adopted that year lasts two months
China requires three subjects to be taught in Mandarin in Inner Mongolia’s Mongolian-language schools; the protests that follow are quickly suppressed
Chagatai Khan begins his rule over the appanage allotted by Genghis Khan
Alghu exploits the Mongol civil war to assert real independence
Qutlugh Khwaja leads a great Chagataid army to the outskirts of Delhi
Eastern nomadic tribes revolt against Tarmashirin and overthrow him
Timur completes his seizure of power in Transoxiana
The Yarkent Khanate is founded as a Chagataid successor state
Batu withdraws to the lower Volga and establishes his ulus
Uzbek Khan begins a reign in which Islam becomes the state religion
Plague strikes Janibeg's army besieging Caffa
Dmitry of Moscow defeats Mamai at the Battle of Kulikovo
Timur defeats Tokhtamysh on the Terek and sacks Sarai
The Great Stand on the Ugra River ends Moscow's tribute
Meñli I Giray of Crimea defeats the last khan and sacks Sarai
Kublai's claim to be Great Khan sparks civil war with his brother Ariq Böke
Kublai Khan adopts the dynastic name Da Yuan
Xiangyang falls to Mongol counterweight trebuchets after a five-year siege
The first Mongol invasion of Japan is wrecked by storms
The last Song loyalist fleet is destroyed at Yamen, leaving the Yuan masters of all China
The Yellow River bursts its dykes, devastating the North China Plain
The Red Turban Rebellion breaks out across the Huai and Yangtze valleys
Zhu Yuanzhang proclaims the Ming and Toghon Temür flees Dadu
Timur's army raises towers of skulls from the population of Isfahan
Timur defeats Tokhtamysh of the Golden Horde on the Terek
Timur sacks Delhi, leaving the city devastated for decades
Timur defeats and captures the Ottoman Sultan Bayezid I at Ankara
Timur dies at Otrar while marching to invade Ming China
Ulugh Beg is put to death at the instigation of his own son
Abu Sa'id, last Timurid to reunite much of the realm, is killed fighting the Aq Qoyunlu
Muhammad Shaybani Khan takes Herat, ending Timurid rule
Zhu Yuanzhang defeats Chen Youliang at the naval battle of Lake Poyang
Zhu Yuanzhang proclaims the Ming dynasty and his armies take the Yuan capital, Dadu
Zheng He's first expedition sets out on voyages that reach East Africa by 1433
The Forbidden City is completed in the Yongle Emperor's new capital, Beijing
The Oirat Mongols capture the Zhengtong Emperor at Tumu
Li Zicheng takes Beijing; the Chongzhen Emperor takes his own life and the Qing occupy the city
The last Southern Ming loyalist regime comes to an end
Yi Seong-gye deposes the last Goryeo king and founds Joseon
King Sejong creates the Korean alphabet
The Gyeongguk daejeon law code is promulgated
Hideyoshi invades; Yi Sun-sin wins at Hansan Island
Injo surrenders to the Qing after the siege of Namhansanseong
The Treaty of Ganghwa opens Korea to Japan
Sho Hashi conquers Nanzan and completes the unification of Okinawa
The 'bridge of all nations' bell is cast for Shuri Castle
Kanemaru takes the throne as Sho En, founding the Second Sho dynasty
Sho Shin's forces defeat Oyake Akahachi and take control of the Yaeyama Islands
Satsuma invades and King Sho Nei surrenders Shuri
Tamagusuku Chokun's kumi odori dance-dramas are first performed for Chinese envoys
Commodore Perry signs a compact with the kingdom at Naha
Japan abolishes the Ryukyu Domain and creates Okinawa Prefecture
Tauekel Khan takes Tashkent and Turkistan from Bukhara
Jahangir Khan checks the Dzungars at the Battle of Orbulaq
Dzungar invasion begins the 'Years of the Great Disaster'
Abulkhair Khan of the Junior Juz swears allegiance to Russia
Russia abolishes the khanship in the Middle Juz
Kenesary Kasymov, the last khan, is killed and his revolt ends
Tokugawa Ieyasu defeats Ishida Mitsunari's western coalition at Sekigahara
The imperial court appoints Ieyasu shogun
The siege of Osaka Castle destroys the Toyotomi house
Iemitsu formalises sankin-kotai, the alternate attendance of daimyo in Edo
Dutch traders are confined to the artificial island of Dejima in Nagasaki
Commodore Perry's 'Black Ships' enter Edo Bay demanding open ports
Shogun Tokugawa Yoshinobu returns governing authority to Emperor Meiji
Imperial rule is restored and the Boshin War begins at Toba-Fushimi
Erdeni Batur joins the assembly that drafts the Mongol-Oirat Code
Galdan conquers the Yarkent Khanate and the Tarim Basin oases
Kangxi's armies defeat Galdan at the Battle of Jao Modo
Dzungar forces under Tsering Dondub sack Lhasa
Dzungar invasion of the Kazakh steppe begins the 'Great Disaster'
Galdan Tseren destroys a Qing army at Hoton Nor
Qing armies reach the Ili valley; Amursana rebels
Nurhaci proclaims the Later Jin dynasty
Hong Taiji proclaims the Qing dynasty
Wu Sangui opens the Shanhai Pass and Qing forces capture Beijing
The Qing conquer Taiwan from the Zheng regime, completing consolidation
The six-year-old Puyi abdicates, ending imperial rule in China
After Nader Shah Afshar's death in June, a loya jirga near Kandahar lasting nine days chooses Ahmad Khan, crowned Padshah, Durr-i-Durran, by the holy man Sabir Khan.
The Mughal Emperor Ahmad Shah Bahadur cedes Sindh, the Punjab and the trans-Indus lands to Ahmad Shah to save his capital from attack.
Ahmad Shah sacks Delhi but leaves the Mughal emperor in nominal control in return for recognising Afghan suzerainty over Punjab, Sindh and Kashmir.
On 14 January the Durranis decisively defeat the Marathas under Sadashivrao Bhau at the Third Battle of Panipat, fought along a twelve-kilometre front.
Ahmad Shah crosses into Punjab for the sixth time, takes Amritsar, massacres thousands of Sikhs in the Vadda Ghallughara and destroys the Golden Temple.
Ahmad Shah dies in the mountains east of Kandahar; after Shah Wali Khan is assassinated at Farah, Timur Shah takes the throne in November.
On 7 June Shuja Shah signs the first Afghan pact with a European power, with the British East India Company; weeks later Mahmud Shah deposes him.
Ayub Shah, the last Sadozai ruler of the empire, is deposed and presumably killed.
Hong Huoxiu fails the imperial examination for the third time and has the visions in which he is given the name Hong Xiuquan
Hong’s follower Feng Yunshan founds the God Worshipping Society in Guangxi
After routing Qing forces at Jintian, Hong declares himself Heavenly King of the Taiping Heavenly Kingdom
The Taipings capture Nanjing, rename it Tianjing and kill its Manchu population
In the Tianjing Incident Yang Xiuqing and his followers are slaughtered on Hong Xiuquan’s orders
Zeng Guofan’s Xiang Army captures Anqing, helped by a Royal Navy blockade
Hong Xiuquan dies during the siege, and Nanjing falls to the imperial armies in the Third Battle of Nanjing
The last Taiping army, led by Li Fuzhong, is wiped out on the borders of Hunan, Guizhou and Guangxi
Commodore Matthew C. Perry’s American expedition reaches Japan with documents requesting an end to Japanese isolation
Ii Naosuke approves the Treaty of Amity and Commerce against the Emperor’s wishes and launches the Ansei Purge
Sakamoto Ryōma brings Kido Takayoshi and Saigō Takamori together to form the Satsuma–Chōshū Alliance
Tokugawa Yoshinobu, the 15th shōgun, returns power to the Imperial Court and resigns the title of shōgun
Domain troops seize the Imperial Palace and the Emperor declares the restoration of his authority, setting off the Boshin War
The daimyō are told that the domains are abolished, and the 302 domains become 72 prefectures in January 1872
Nationwide conscription extends the right to bear arms, once a samurai privilege, to every man
The Meiji Constitution is adopted; it remains in place until the Allied occupation after the Second World War
The Zongli Yamen is created under Prince Gong to conduct relations with the Western powers
The Tongwen Guan opens in Beijing to train interpreters, later adding mathematics and astronomy
Zeng Guofan and Li Hongzhang found the Jiangnan Arsenal at Shanghai
Zuo Zongtang founds the Fuzhou Navy Yard and its naval school
The China Merchants’ Steam Navigation Company is founded; the first Educational Mission students sail for America
A French squadron destroys the Fujian fleet at Fuzhou in the Sino-French War
The Beiyang Fleet is formally established under Admiral Ding Ruchang
Defeated by Japan, the Qing sign the Treaty of Shimonoseki
Meiji Restoration overthrows the Tokugawa shogunate after some 265 years
Meiji Constitution establishes a constitutional monarchy with an Imperial Diet
First Sino-Japanese War begins, ending in Japanese victory over Qing China in 1895
Admiral Togo annihilates the Russian fleet at Tsushima, sealing victory over Russia
Army officers stage the Mukden Incident, launching independent action in Manchuria
US oil embargo in August pushes Japan towards the attack on Pearl Harbor
Japan loses four fleet carriers at Midway, surrendering the strategic initiative
After Hiroshima, Nagasaki and Soviet entry into the war, Japan surrenders aboard USS Missouri
The Wuchang Uprising on 10 October begins the Xinhai Revolution
Sun Yat-sen becomes provisional president at Nanjing; the last Qing emperor abdicates
The Northern Expedition takes Beijing and the Nationalists reunify much of China
War with Japan begins after the Marco Polo Bridge Incident
Defeated in the civil war, the government moves to Taipei
UN Resolution 2758 transfers China’s seat to the People’s Republic
Martial law on Taiwan is lifted after 38 years
First direct presidential election, won by Lee Teng-hui
Japan’s Twenty-One Demands become known to the Chinese public and provoke anti-Japanese feeling
China enters World War I on the side of the Triple Entente, and Hu Shih argues for the vernacular in “Preliminary discussion on literary reform”
The leak of the secret Sino-Japanese Joint Defence Agreement signed by Premier Duan Qirui sparks a student protest movement
On May 4 over 4,000 students gather in front of Tiananmen to protest the Shandong terms of the Treaty of Versailles
After the June 3 arrests a general strike in Shanghai forces the dismissal of Cao Rulin, Zhang Zongxiang and Lu Zongyu, and China’s delegates refuse to sign the treaty
Chen Duxiu and Li Dazhao are among the founders of the Chinese Communist Party
Mao Zedong calls the May Fourth Movement a new stage in China’s bourgeois-democratic revolution
After the Mukden incident and the Japanese invasion of Manchuria in 1931, Manchukuo is proclaimed on 18 February and formally established at Xinjing on 1 March, with Puyi as nominal head of state.
On 15 September Japan recognises the state through the Japan–Manchukuo Protocol; the Manchukuo Imperial Army is founded by the Army and Navy Act of 15 April.
The League of Nations endorses the Lytton Report in February, finding Japan had broken international law; Japan withdraws from the League.
On 1 March Manchukuo is proclaimed a monarchy and Puyi takes the throne with the era name Kangde; El Salvador, the Dominican Republic and Costa Rica recognise the state.
Five Year Plans modelled on the Soviet Union's begin; Nobusuke Kishi, deputy minister since 1935, brings the zaibatsu into a state-directed heavy industry.
Manchukuo serves as the base for Japan's invasion of the rest of China after the Marco Polo Bridge incident; 'thought crime' is introduced and an emergency law mobilises society for total war.
A border skirmish between Manchukuoan and Mongolian cavalry in May escalates into the Battles of Khalkhin Gol, where a Soviet–Mongolian force defeats the Kwantung Army.
The Soviet Union declares war on 8 August and invades; Manchukuo units surrender or mutiny, Puyi abdicates on 17 August and is captured by the Soviets.
The May Fourth Movement begins with 3,000 students in Beijing protesting the Versailles Treaty’s concessions to Japan
Mao’s pamphlet Strategic Problems of China’s Revolutionary War marks his turn away from the Soviet model
The Communist Party’s 7th national congress makes Mao Zedong Thought its unified ideology and writes it into the party constitution
The famines that follow the Great Leap Forward begin; by some historians’ count thirty million die by 1961
The Naxalbari uprising in India begins the Naxalite movement, which spreads Quotations from Chairman Mao Zedong
China announces its Three Worlds Theory at the United Nations
Deng Xiaoping begins market reforms and calls the true spirit of Mao Zedong Thought “seeking truth from facts”
The party’s resolution on its history holds Mao chiefly responsible for the Cultural Revolution while upholding his Thought
Mao Zedong proclaims the People’s Republic in Beijing on 1 October
Chinese People’s Volunteers enter the Korean War
The Great Leap Forward begins, leading to the famine of 1959–61
The People’s Republic takes China’s seat at the United Nations
Deng Xiaoping launches reform and opening
The army crushes the Tiananmen Square protests on 4 June
China joins the World Trade Organization
Uzbekistan declares independence on 31 August after the failed coup in Moscow; Islam Karimov is elected president on 29 December.
The Oliy Majlis replaces the Supreme Soviet, the Republican Stock Exchange opens and Uzbekistan applies to join the World Trade Organization.
After the 11 September attacks Uzbekistan grants the United States access to the Karshi-Khanabad airfield for operations in Afghanistan.
Government troops fire into crowds of protesters in Andijan, killing 187 by official count and several hundred by witness accounts; the United States is ordered to leave Karshi-Khanabad.
The Afrosiyob high-speed train between Tashkent and Samarkand, the first in Central Asia, makes its first trip on 26 August.
Karimov dies on 2 September; Prime Minister Shavkat Mirziyoyev is elected president with 88.6 percent of the vote and sworn in on 14 December.
In September the som becomes fully convertible at market rates, ending the chief barrier to foreign business.
The United Nations announces 'major progress' against forced labour in the cotton harvest, with 94 percent of pickers working voluntarily.
